Hi Rajesh / Elena —

Thanks — attached is our completed questionnaire (PDF) plus a short runbook extract that highlights the multi-region cutover sequence and KV prefix-warming steps. Summary of the key commitments below; full answers are in the attachment and the Drive link I've shared. Happy to walk through these on a call.

High-level commitments (hosted / dedicated / private):
- Hosted (Redwood API): RTO target = 15 minutes for progressive multi-region cutover (see sequencing below); RPO target = < 10 minutes for customer-specific metadata and state. Application-visible session state may be transient for a short period during cutover; we rely on request-side idempotency for critical flows.
- Dedicated (reserved pools): RTO target = 15 minutes for automatic region failover when using our cross-region warm standby configuration; RPO = near-zero to 5 minutes when customers enable our streaming replication (recommended for stateful workloads).
- Private (VPC / on-prem): RTO / RPO depend on customer-managed replication topology. We provide runbook steps, replication tooling, and a best-practice template; typical on-prem customers plan for RTO <= 1 hour with RPO variable (customer-controlled).

Failover sequencing (progressive cutover we recommend):
1) Detect and declare incident; failover coordinator assigns regional owners.
2) Bring up control-plane components in secondary region (0–3m).
3) Start warm standby serving pool with model weights and KV cache snapshot restore (3–9m).
4) Progressive traffic ramp (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with health checks and prefix warming hooks (9–15m).

Data replication model:
- Metadata and persistent customer objects: streamed to secondary region via async change-log with guaranteed-once consumer and per-customer checkpoints.
- In-flight KV cache: we persist periodic snapshots and ship deltas during steady state; full warmup happens during step 3 above.

Cache warming & request routing notes:
- We use prefix-aware cache warming: key prefixes for frequent endpoints are restored first and traffic is routed with a short cold-cache tolerance.
- For latency-sensitive customers, we recommend enabling our per-customer KV replication to reduce first-request cold penalties.

Kim / team — quick confirmations and a small amendment to the PDF I'm attaching. TL;DR: yes, we can commit to the wording below with two clarifying caveats.

1) Dedicated RPO <= 5 minutes: Confirmed for customers who provision the streaming replication option. This is a standard configuration that we ship and support; it requires enabling the cross-region change-log consumer and a small buffer for replay (we document monitoring thresholds). Caveat: for extremely high write-rate workloads (>= 10k writes/s), we recommend an engineering review; we still hit sub-5m RPO in most cases but reserve the right to add guidance around sharding replication streams.

2) KV warmup window (hosted): The 3–9 minute window assumes a median KV dataset (tens of millions of keys) and parallelized snapshot restore. For very large KV footprints (hundreds of millions of keys) warmup will extend — realistically 20–45 minutes — unless customers enable per-customer incremental replication. I've updated the runbook text to call this out and added a recovery-time matrix in the attached runbook-extract.

Other small edits included: explicit statement that control-plane failover (DNS and routing update) is typically sub-60s once the coordinator declares the region switch, and that can be a gating step if downstream CDNs or corporate DNS TTLs are high.
